analysis.one_liner: Suspends the federal gas tax whenever gasoline tops $3.99 a gallon, and suspends oil companies' tax breaks during those months.
analysis.headline: No vote: the bill, with 9 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and none from the other party, has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee since its referral on April 30, 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: Whenever the national average gasoline price exceeds $3.99 per gallon, the bill would cut the federal fuel excise tax by one cent for every cent the price is above that threshold — so at $4.99 a gallon, the roughly 18-cent federal tax would be fully suspended. To keep road and leaky-underground-tank programs whole, it would transfer general taxpayer money to those trust funds. During the same high-price months, oil and gas companies would lose three tax breaks: the intangible drilling cost deduction, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and the marginal well credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers benefit at the pump during months when gas averages above $3.99: the federal excise tax (about 18.4 cents per gallon) is progressively reduced, up to a full suspension. Highway and underground storage tank programs keep their funding because the Treasury replaces the lost revenue from the general fund.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the federal fuel excise tax by one cent for every cent the national average gasoline price exceeds $3.99, reaching a full suspension of the tax (about 18.4 cents per gallon) when prices are roughly $4.17 or higher.

Requires the Treasury to transfer general-fund money to the Highway Trust Fund and the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund equal to the revenue lost, so road projects and tank-cleanup work are not cut.

Suspends oil and gas companies' intangible drilling cost deduction, enhanced oil recovery credit, and marginal well credit for costs and production during the same high-price months, partially paying for the consumer relief.

analysis.who_pays: The general fund — meaning all federal taxpayers or the deficit — pays to make the highway and tank-cleanup trust funds whole, and oil and gas companies lose three tax breaks for any costs or production during high-price months.

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts the tax but contains no requirement that refiners, wholesalers, or stations pass the savings on to drivers, so some or all of the relief could be absorbed by companies in the supply chain instead.

The savings are capped: a driver can save no more than the federal tax itself, about 18.4 cents per gallon, no matter how high prices go, and the benefit arrives only in months when the national average — not any individual's local price — exceeds $3.99.
Replacing the trust-fund revenue with general-fund transfers means the relief is deficit-financed, shifting the cost to all federal taxpayers rather than only to those who buy fuel.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Drivers get real but modest, capped relief — at most about 18 cents a gallon, and only if stations pass it through, which the bill does not require. The offsetting clawback from oil companies is real but applies only in high-price months, and the trust-fund make-whole means the true cost lands on the general fund. It is a targeted consumer-relief bill more than a structural fix for fuel prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced the bill on April 30, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax bills.
Eight House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote has occurred, and the Congress is still in session, so the bill remains in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep their drilling deductions and credits, and drivers have gotten no relief; the Ways and Means chair avoids having to vote on an industry tax clawback.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies keep their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Brendan Boyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee has taken no action on the bill since referral — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: 223 of 223 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No member cosponsored or acted to advance the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; not a single Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a Republican-controlled committee.

industries.note: The bill would take away three targeted tax breaks — the intangible drilling cost deduction, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and the marginal well credit — during any month gas prices exceed $3.99. That is exactly when producer revenues run highest, so the provision is aimed at clawing back windfall-period subsidies.

Suspending the fuel excise tax would normally drain the Highway Trust Fund that pays for road work, but the bill replaces every lost dollar from the general fund, so construction programs are protected while the cost shifts to general taxpayers.

Lower pump prices during high-price months would tend to lift fuel demand, but the bill imposes no pass-through requirement, leaving retailers and wholesalers free to keep the suspended tax as margin.

analysis.trajectory: Most private-member tax bills introduced without bipartisan support die quietly in the Ways and Means Committee. With no Republican cosponsors and a Republican chair who has not scheduled action, this bill is very likely to expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, unless it is folded into a larger tax package.
